title: State legislative offices responded to machine-generated policy emails at nearly the same rate as human-written emails
source_unit: Kreps and Kriner randomized field experiment on state legislative offices
geography: United States state legislators; legislators in more than 40 states received experimental emails

denominator.unit: emails sent to state legislators; approximately five per legislator, randomized across human/GPT-3 text, six issues, and ideological direction

human_response_rate.unit: percent of human-written policy emails receiving a legislative response

ai_response_rate.unit: percent of GPT-3-generated policy emails receiving a legislative response

response_gap.unit: percentage points, AI-generated minus human-written; statistically significant but substantively modest

response_length.value: median 322 words for human-written replies versus 272 words for machine-generated replies; interquartile ranges were nearly identical

issue_variation.value: response rates were nearly identical on gun control and health policy; machine-generated messages had a nonsignificantly higher rate on education and lower rates on policing, reproductive rights, and taxes

observations.method: The researchers randomly alternated human-written and GPT-3-generated advocacy emails across six policy issues and conservative/liberal positions, then coded whether offices responded and the length of replies. The messages used aliases and the study was an audit of office responsiveness rather than a survey of constituents.
observations.uncertainty: This is a deceptive audit experiment involving state legislators, not Members of Congress; response is an intermediate proxy for attention or priority, not substantive policy action, issue resolution, or constituent benefit. The experiment occurred during the 2020 pandemic/election environment, and the paper cautions that federal-legislator generalization is uncertain.
observations.subgroup: State legislative offices across issue and ideological conditions; the article reports different AI-human gaps by issue and party, but does not make those exploratory interactions a population estimate.
observations.counterinterpretation: A reply can be automated, generic, or strategically noncommittal; similar response rates do not mean equal authenticity detection, equal influence, or equal representation. Lower response to AI text may reflect detectable inconsistencies, while higher-volume synthetic correspondence could still distort the apparent distribution of public opinion.

related_sources.claim: The research record identifies the field experiment and reports the small aggregate response-rate difference.

boundary: This record closes a randomized message-to-office-response layer for state legislative policy correspondence. It does not establish ordinary constituent access, response quality, policy change, issue resolution, trust recovery, or national congressional responsiveness.

reproduction_audit.retrieval_hash_scope: Cornell-hosted article PDF downloaded and hashed; SSRN record and article text cross-checked.
